blocks.cap: Rei on the long way down to the river

blocks.p: Rei walked to the river the long way, because Gin's map said the long way was the honest one.

It was the evening before the last night of Obon. The heat of the day had not gone anywhere. It sat in the streets like water in a bath that nobody had let out. The cicadas were still going in the shrine trees behind the flat, a hard dry noise that rose and fell, and Rei could feel his shirt stick to his back before he reached the end of the lane. On almost every doorstep there was a paper lantern, white or pale blue, hung for the dead who had come home for the week. Some families had already set out little trays for the fires of the next night. Nobody looked at him. Everyone was busy with their own dead.

He went down past Jūjō Station first. The green-striped Saikyō line trains came and went. On the southbound platform there was a patch of floor, about the size of a bath mat, that was always a little cold. It was a weak thin spot, and Gin's notes said it had been there since at least 1998. It was too small to do harm. Commuters stepped around it every day without knowing why. Rei watched a man in a white shirt do it now, a small sideways step with his eyes on his phone, and then the man stood on the warm side of the line and waited for his train as if nothing had happened.

Rei touched his Suica card to the gate. It beeped. He took the Saikyō line one stop north to Akabane. The carriage was half full. A woman fanned herself with a folded train timetable. Two schoolgirls in summer uniforms shared one pair of earphones, a wire each, and laughed at the same moment at something only they could hear. An old man near the door held a bundle wrapped in a purple furoshiki, and from the shape of it Rei guessed it held offerings for a family grave. Fruit, maybe, or a box of sweets. The man held it on his knees with both hands the whole way, very carefully, as if it might spill.

At Akabane he came out of the station and turned into Ichibangai. Ichibangai is a tangle of narrow streets beside the station, packed with tiny bars and standing counters and yakitori grills, some of them open since the morning. Gin had written that these drinking streets were so loud with warm, ordinary feeling that two people could talk there and no Clairsentient in the ward could pick their words out. Rei did not need to talk to anyone. He needed one last stretch of noise to stand in.

So he stood in it. Smoke from the grills hung under the paper lanterns. Salarymen with their ties pulled loose sat elbow to elbow on beer crates. Someone was singing badly behind a curtain, and a whole room was clapping to keep him going. Rei let it wash over him for ten minutes. It felt like standing under a warm shower. Then he turned south and began to walk toward Ōji.

He walked along the tracks of the Keihin-Tōhoku line. The sky-blue trains passed him every few minutes, bright and full and humming. He went past Higashi-Jūjō, past shut shops and lit vending machines, past a konbini where a tired student was stacking rice balls into the cold shelf. The sky over the rooftops went from orange to purple to a dirty dark blue. The air did not cool at all.
Then the ground rose beside the tracks, and he was at Asukayama.

Gin had warned about Asukayama. The park held the old city in it the way cloth holds a smell. Three hundred years of picnics, blossom, executions and lovers, all pressed into one hill. To someone who could read the dead, it was so dense that a quiet lawn sounded like a crowd. Not hostile, Gin had written. Just loud. A single-car tram of the Toden Arakawa line ground its way up the slope beside the park, lit inside like a small kitchen, with three passengers looking at nothing. Rei kept his registers closed and went past the hill with his head down.

Below Ōji the streets flattened out into the Kita-Ōji yards. These were low pre-war sheds, rail sidings and loading bays, all shuttered for the festival. Long ago many people had suffered here, and the Grid had never cleared it. Here the old misery lay in the corrugated walls and the oil-black ground in long, untreated bands. Gin's map marked the whole district in pencil with two words. Likeliest crossing.
Tonight Rei could feel why. All those bands of old misery were leaning the same way, toward the water. They leaned like iron filings lean toward a magnet.
He came up the embankment toward the wound. The air over the river was doing what Higuchi had warned it would do. The bookseller had written about this night in his smallest, most frightened letters.

The air was thinning. It was thin the way the skin over a knuckle goes thin and tight when a person makes a fist. Rei could see the far bank. He could also see a second far bank through it, one that was not there. It was as if two cities had been laid on top of each other, and one of them had slipped a little out of place.

Below him on the near bank stood the riverside memorial, with flowers all around it. People called this the March ground. Every year the grief of the eleventh of March came here and settled, like mud settling at the bottom of a pond. An old woman in a flowered apron was changing the water in the vases by the light of a torch. She did not look up. She was speaking quietly to the river.

An hour earlier the neighbourhood had floated paper lanterns on the water. They were still going downstream, little orange lights on the black river. Rei let his suppressed registers come halfway up, just enough to look. Behind every lantern there was a second light, and the second light did not move with the current. It was something on the other side, leaning close to watch the small fires the living send to guide their dead home. Leaning close and holding its breath.

That was the obscene part. It was beautiful. The wall was failing, and the failure looked like a festival. Rei understood at last why the Healer had chosen Obon. It was not for the cover of the crowds. It was because during these few nights the whole city agrees to call the thinning of the wall a kindness.
Gin was already there.

He stood at the rail where the embankment path turned. He wore the grey cardigan he had worn all month, the one Rei could no longer look at without his throat closing. His long black hair hung loose past his jaw, and the river wind moved it a little. He was looking at the doubled river.
Rei had learned to read his brother's face in two layers, like everything else about him now.

Underneath was Gin. Tired, frightened and trying. That layer came up when the thing wearing him loosened its grip to let the body rest. Over it, calm and attentive and almost tender, was the Healer. Yushiro, the demon of Duty. If anyone had ever caught a demon between two skins, the registry would have given it a number. It turned his brother's face toward the wound the way a surgeon turns a calm face toward an open chest.

Every instrument in the CVD had read that register as stillness. Its machines had found no feeling in the Healer at all. They called it null-emotive and filed it under the thirteenth register, XIII, as an empty space. Only one archivist, in an entry twenty-two years old and buried in Yamamoto's stacks, had ever written down the right word, and nobody upstairs had believed it. Rei had felt the Healer in his kitchen, on his phone, and across a table at the Far-Shore house. He knew what it was now. It was not empty. It was a feeling so complete that there was no room in it for anything else.
Both of them turned when they heard Rei on the gravel. Both of them, in the same body, were glad he had come. The two kinds of gladness were the worst thing he had ever had to look at.

"You found the registry," Gin said. It was the Healer's even voice coming out of his brother's mouth, and it was not a question. "I hoped you would. I left the shelf unlocked for you. The one door this whole month that did not lock itself. You noticed that. You notice everything. It is the best of you, and it is why I could never have done this with anyone else holding the other end."

He waved a hand at the doubled river, the lanterns, the thin bright seam where two cities almost touched. It was a gentle gesture, like a teacher showing a pupil the one diagram that explains the whole lesson.

"So you know what this is. You know there is a chair. You know it has stood open since the year the lights went grey. And you know, because you are the only person left alive who can feel both sides of a thing at once, that an open chair does not stay open. It only waits for the two who can close it. We are both here. The waiting is the part that is over."
Rei never had to answer. The cult answered for him.

Someone came up the far embankment, on the other side of the wound. It was a young man in a courier's jacket, as thin as a coat hanger. He walked with a loose, obedient step, like a body that had been emptied and filled again with something else. Kaito. The boy who preached in the drained pool. Kishin's mouth. Rei had hunted him through the city for days and never cornered him. He did not come now as an ambush. He came like the second guest at an appointment.

Behind Kaito's eyes something else looked out across the water. Rei knew its weight from the Far-Shore house in Takinogawa, from the tea and the white rooms and the wall of photographs of the missing. It was Kishin. The demon of Despair that wore the body of a dead woman, Fukai Rinka, and called itself Kanna-sensei. It was the thing eating Watanabe Jun's seat out from under him, and growing toward becoming the Inverted God, the dark mirror of the Axis. It did not need to come itself tonight. It had sent its mouth to watch.
Seeing it there, across the thin bright seam from the Healer, rearranged the whole month in Rei's chest at once.

The two demons were not on the same side. They did not even want the same thing. But with the river doubled between them and the lanterns burning down, Rei saw that they had been working on the same wound from two ends. The Healer had thinned the wall along its grain. Kishin's Circle had cleared away every medium in the ward who might have noticed. And both of them had come out on the thin night. Whatever the chair was for, the trap had always been built for two brothers.
One brother to fill the seat. One brother to be the cost of filling it. The Healer had never needed to defeat Rei. It only needed them both here, alive, on the thin night, loving each other.
"Now you see the second jaw," the Healer said. There was no triumph in it. That was the unbearable part. His brother's voice, used by the thing, sounded sorry.

"I told you the truth at every step, because the truth was the trap. I did not have to lie to a man who notices everything. I only had to let him notice in order. The wall thins these nights no matter what either of us does. That work is six years done. It was done before you could read a ward. What is still open is the chair, and a chair this old closes for one of two living things keyed to it. You."
He did not point at himself. He let the silence say the second name.

"Or the body I am standing in. One register goes into the seat, and the office is filled, and the wall is mended, and the twelve stop being crushed, and Watanabe sleeps for the first time in a decade. And one register is left over, on the embankment, alive, to spend the rest of a life knowing it could have been the other way. That is the whole of it. There is no third thing across the river except the one that has come to make sure neither of us walks away from the chair. That is what the cult's friend is for. It is the lock on the door I have already opened."

Across the water Kaito smiled with a mouth that did not belong to him. It was the smile of something that wanted the chair to stay empty a little longer. It was happy to watch two brothers argue over it while the wall wore thin.
Then, under the Healer's calm, for one breath, Rei's real brother came up.

Rei felt it happen. It was like a swimmer breaking the surface of the water, sudden and desperate, without asking permission. Gin's hands moved before his mouth did. His right thumb pressed the knuckles of his left hand in a quick order, one, three, two. Then the heel of his hand went flat against his breastbone. To anyone watching, it was a tired man rubbing his hands against the chill off the river. But Rei had read the chapter on glyphs that morning. He knew a key when he saw one turned. Gin had marks inked into his skin, and that small movement woke one of them. Something on his brother's forearm, under the cardigan, grew warm. For the length of one sentence, the Healer lost its grip on his tongue.
Gin looked at Rei across the lanterns with his own eyes. He spoke fast and low, in the voice that had read stories to Rei when he was small.

"Rei. Don't let it be you. Whatever it says, however right it makes the arithmetic sound, the chair is the thing it wants, and it does not care which of us sits in it, and that means the one it is steering you toward is you. Let it be me. I am already most of the way gone. Let it..."

Then the Healer took the tongue back. Smoothly. Without hurry. The way a man takes a pen out of a child's hand. Gin's hands went still at his sides. They went still on purpose, the way they had always gone still when he was thinking. And the calm, sorry teacher was looking at Rei again.
The river ran doubled and bright between everything Rei still had to decide.
